claim: Rolling back in an AFTER trigger is expensive since data is changed twice; a table allows only one INSTEAD OF trigger per action; IF UPDATE(column) limits the check to changed columns.

sources.apa: Microsoft. (n.d.). CREATE TRIGGER (Transact-SQL) - SQL Server. Microsoft Learn. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/create-trigger-transact-sql
sources.verified_via: Direct fetch of the Microsoft Learn page (no DOI); page ms.date 2025-09-26
sources.supports: States 'At most, you can define one INSTEAD OF trigger per INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement on a table or view'; states UPDATE() tests for UPDATE or INSERT attempts on one column (COLUMNS_UPDATED for several); AFTER trigger runs only after the triggering statement has succeeded; example C uses AFTER INSERT with ROLLBACK.

notes: No academic source found stating SQL Server-specific trigger rules, so vendor fallback. The page does NOT state the sentence 'rolling back in an AFTER trigger is expensive since the data is changed twice'; it only says AFTER triggers fire after the statement has succeeded (so a ROLLBACK undoes work already done) and that triggers hold locks until commit/rollback. Treat the 'expensive' wording as the report's own inference, or soften it. Page applies to SQL Server 2017-2025.
main_session_decision: Vendor fallback only (Microsoft Learn). "AFTER rollback is expensive" sentence to lose its citation.

claim: In SQL Server a function cannot insert into tables (UDFs cannot modify database state); functions cannot have output parameters; procedure uses a table-valued parameter.

sources.apa: Microsoft. (n.d.). CREATE FUNCTION (Transact-SQL) - SQL Server. Microsoft Learn. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/create-function-transact-sql
sources.verified_via: Direct fetch of the Microsoft Learn page (no DOI); page ms.date 2025-11-03
sources.supports: Limitations section: 'User-defined functions can't be used to perform actions that modify the database state'; function_body must not produce side effects such as modifying a table; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE allowed only on local table variables; READONLY is required for user-defined table type (TVP) parameters.

notes: No academic source found, so vendor fallback. The page does not literally say 'functions cannot have output parameters'; the function syntax simply has no OUTPUT option for parameters and the only parameter modifier is READONLY. Cite it for the side-effect rule and TVP READONLY; the output-parameter point is an inference from the syntax. Page applies to SQL Server 2017-2025.

claim: Exclusive locks held until commit; locking does not prevent deadlocks (2PL)

sources.apa: Eswaran, K. P., Gray, J. N., Lorie, R. A., & Traiger, I. L. (1976). The notions of consistency and predicate locks in a database system. Communications of the ACM, 19(11), 624-633. https://doi.org/10.1145/360363.360369
sources.supports: Introduces two-phase locking as the rule that guarantees consistent (serialisable) schedules, and discusses deadlock as a consequence of locking.
sources.older_than_5y_reason: Foundational: original two-phase locking paper. Recent hits (2021-2025) were narrow protocol or niche-journal papers, not general statements of the claim.

notes: Strict 2PL (hold exclusive locks to commit) is a later refinement; Eswaran et al. states 2PL itself. Optional recent alternative of lower quality: Kafr El-Sheikh J. Inf. Sci. 2022 review, doi 10.21608/kjis.2022.246104 (not verified in detail, not recommended).
main_session_decision: Foundational 1976 paper (5-year exception); cite for locking and deadlock, not strict 2PL.
